name: Citalopram
route_note: Oral tablets or solution once daily; IV formulation available in some countries.

discovery.note: A racemic bicyclic phthalane derivative; its S-enantiomer was later developed as escitalopram.

tagline: Racemic SSRI from Lundbeck, limited by dose-dependent QT prolongation
summary: Citalopram is a racemic SSRI used for depression. Developed by Lundbeck and marketed in the US by Forest Laboratories as Celexa, it is among the most selective SSRIs. Its S-enantiomer, escitalopram, carries most of the therapeutic activity.
mechanism: Citalopram is a highly selective inhibitor of the serotonin transporter with minimal effects on noradrenaline and dopamine uptake and low affinity for other receptors. The S-enantiomer is responsible for SERT inhibition; the R-enantiomer is much weaker and may counteract S-citalopram binding via an allosteric site.
Dose-dependent prolongation of the QT interval led regulators to limit the maximum daily dose.

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: Citalopram is synthesised at Lundbeck in Copenhagen.

history.title: First approval
history.detail: Citalopram is launched in Denmark as Cipramil.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: The FDA approves Celexa (Forest Laboratories) for depression.

history.title: Generics
history.detail: Generic citalopram becomes available in the US.

history.title: QT warning
history.detail: The FDA warns of dose-dependent QT prolongation and limits the maximum dose to 40 mg/day (20 mg in older people).

history.title: EU restriction
history.detail: European regulators similarly restrict the maximum dose after QT review.

pk.metabolism: Hepatic CYP2C19, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 to desmethylcitalopram
pk.excretion: Renal and hepatic; ~12% unchanged in urine

serious: QT prolongation and torsade de pointes
safety.boxed_warning: Increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours in children, adolescents and young adults (under 25) taking antidepressants; monitor for clinical worsening.

facts: Citalopram is one of the most selective SSRIs for SERT over other transporters.
Its development led directly to the single-enantiomer escitalopram.
